summary: Integrations get an identity of their own, a limited set of permissions, and keys that can be rotated. A team can take away one person's access without breaking the company's automations.
scope_note: A made-up scenario, used to judge the interface. No real repository was analysed and no tests were run.

decision.label: Conditionally, into the core
decision.rationale: The product direction holds up. Before merging, the domain has to be separated from the key store, and a migration for existing integrations has to be agreed.

conditions.title: A port instead of direct SQL
conditions.verification: Auth depends on KeyResolver; the SQL adapter stays outside the domain. The domain test runs without a database.

conditions.title: Migration without cutting anyone off
conditions.verification: An agreed transition period, a message to customers, and a clear condition for switching personal tokens off.

conditions.title: Tenant isolation and revocation
conditions.verification: Tests across organizations, plus a test that a revoked key stops working immediately, with the run's result recorded.

capabilities.title: Organization keys
capabilities.before: An integration runs on an employee's token.
capabilities.after: An admin gives the integration its own key and its own permissions.
capabilities.impact: The automation no longer depends on one particular person still being there.

capabilities.title: Permissions per integration
capabilities.before: A token inherits whatever the user can do.
capabilities.after: The Policy Engine judges the organization and the key's permissions.
capabilities.impact: Narrower access, but a new way for one tenant's data to leak into another's.

capabilities.title: Personal token as a fallback
capabilities.before: An older client still works with a user's token.
capabilities.after: The integration path requires an organization identity.
capabilities.impact: Existing integrations have to be migrated before the fallback is switched off.

capabilities.title: Keys expire without anyone remembering
capabilities.before: A token stayed valid until a person deleted it, and the plaintext stayed in the database next to the user.
capabilities.after: An organization key is hashed at rest, rotated on a schedule, and its expiry is announced on the audit stream.
capabilities.impact: Removes the long-lived plaintext credential, and adds a scheduled writer that has to agree with manual revocation.

architecture.headline: A new identity. The same permissions engine.
architecture.description: Two readings of the same change. The authorization path shows what now decides a request; the lifecycle view shows who owns the credential and what is stored.

nodes.label: Admin Console
nodes.after: Creates, rotates and revokes organization keys.
nodes.impact: A new admin surface. Users need to be told what the permissions mean and what revoking one does.

nodes.label: Auth Service
nodes.before: Identifies the user from a token and passes them to the policy engine.
nodes.after: Identifies the organization and its permissions, reading the key straight from the SQL adapter.
nodes.impact: A new tie from the core to infrastructure. If the key store is down, integrations lose access.

nodes.label: Policy Engine
nodes.before: Judges what the signed-in user may do.
nodes.after: Also judges an integration's identity inside its organization.
nodes.impact: One shared policy stays in one place. Isolation between organizations and the absence of permission creep both still need proving.

nodes.label: Personal-token fallback
nodes.before: Maps a personal token to a user for older integrations.
nodes.impact: A breaking change for customers still on the fallback. No transition period has been agreed.

nodes.label: Org Key Registry
nodes.after: Stores the hashed key, the organization, the permissions and whether it has been revoked.
nodes.impact: A new infrastructure responsibility, needing a data migration and a stated plan for when it is unavailable. Suggested port: KeyResolver.

nodes.label: Audit Log
nodes.before: Receives admin events through the shared audit mechanism.
nodes.after: Also receives key.created, key.rotated and key.revoked, with no change to the module itself.
nodes.impact: The code is untouched, but new events arrive. Check what is redacted and who reads the audit trail.

nodes.label: Rotation Worker
nodes.before: Nothing expired a credential. A personal token lived until somebody deleted the account.
nodes.after: Expires and re-issues organization keys on a schedule, writing the new hash and an audit entry.
nodes.impact: A second writer now touches the key registry, so a scheduled rotation and a manual revocation can race.

nodes.label: Secret Store
nodes.before: Personal tokens sat in plaintext columns next to the user row.
nodes.after: Keeps only the hash of a key; the plaintext is shown once at creation and never stored.
nodes.impact: The database stops holding usable credentials, at the cost of a key nobody can recover if the admin loses it.

nodes.label: Notification Service
nodes.before: Sends account-level mail to one named person.
nodes.after: Untouched by the PR, but now receives expiry events addressed to an organization rather than a person.
nodes.impact: An unchanged consumer inherits a new audience; who actually receives an organization-level alert is not settled.

views.title: Authorization path
views.description: A map of parts, not of separately deployed services. The new key store lands on the critical path for authorization, while deciding what is allowed still belongs to the Policy Engine.
views.before_caption: User identity · depends on one employee's account

views.title: Key lifecycle and ownership
views.description: The same change seen from the data side: who issues a key, what is actually stored, and which untouched consumer starts hearing about organizations instead of people.
views.before_caption: Personal tokens · plaintext at rest, no expiry
views.after_caption: Organization keys · hashed at rest, rotated on a schedule

flows.title: An integration calls the API
flows.outcome: Who the caller is changes; deciding what they may do stays in one place.
flows.failure: A new thing that can break: the key store. A timeout should refuse the request rather than let it through, and that behaviour needs a test.

steps.label: Check the key and the tenant

flows.title: Taking an integration's access away
flows.outcome: Revoking one key should not switch off any of the others.
flows.failure: Not known: can a revoked key still be accepted from a cache? Proving revocation works is a condition of this review.

steps.label: Every integration on it stops too

tradeoffs.title: Integrations that stand on their own
tradeoffs.pro: Someone leaving the team no longer breaks the company's automations.
tradeoffs.con: Older integrations have to be moved off personal tokens.
tradeoffs.alternative: A period where both work, with usage figures for the fallback and a date for switching it off.

tradeoffs.title: Reading the key the simple way
tradeoffs.pro: One place holds the truth about permissions and revocation.
tradeoffs.con: Auth becomes tied to SQL; if the store is down, integrations stop.
tradeoffs.alternative: A KeyResolver port in the domain and the SQL adapter in infrastructure, so the behaviour on failure stays explicit.

tradeoffs.title: Giving out the least access needed
tradeoffs.pro: Each integration gets only the permissions it needs.
tradeoffs.con: More authorization states, and more room to confuse one tenant with another.
tradeoffs.alternative: One shared Policy Engine with contract tests covering both kinds of identity.

fit.title: Product direction
fit.rule: Assumed for this example: business integrations are managed at the organization level.
fit.assessment: Organization keys serve that goal, and this is a platform feature rather than an integration with one particular vendor.

fit.title: Domain boundaries
fit.rule: Assumed for this example: a domain module depends on a port, not on a SQL adapter.
fit.assessment: Reading SQL straight from Auth breaks that boundary. Move the dependency onto a KeyResolver interface.

fit.title: One shared access policy
fit.rule: Assumed for this example: every access decision belongs to the Policy Engine.
fit.assessment: The PR extends the existing engine instead of building a second permissions mechanism beside it.

fit.title: Are customers ready to migrate
fit.rule: There is no data on how many current integrations use personal tokens.
fit.assessment: No date for removing the fallback can be approved without that data and a plan for telling customers.

questions.question: Can the fallback be removed in this same release?
questions.why: We do not know how many customers would have to migrate.

questions.question: What does authorization do when the key store times out?
questions.why: A new infrastructure dependency has landed on the critical path.

api_changes.name: Authorization: Bearer <personal token> on /api/*
api_changes.impact: Integrations that still send an employee's personal token are refused once the compatibility path is gone.
api_changes.before: Any /api/* route accepts a personal token and acts as that employee.
api_changes.after: Only organization keys are accepted; a personal token answers 401.
api_changes.migration: Create an organization key in the console, replace the personal token in every integration, then confirm the audit log shows no personal-token calls.

api_changes.name: X-Org-Key request header
api_changes.after: X-Org-Key: <key id>.<secret> identifies the organization and its scopes.

api_changes.name: org_key.rotated / org_key.revoked
api_changes.after: Emitted on every rotation and revocation, carrying the key id and the actor.

api_changes.name: KeyResolver port
api_changes.impact: The made-up PR does not say whether third-party auth plugins must implement the new port.

api_changes.name: org_keys table
api_changes.after: org_keys(id, org_id, scopes, hash, rotated_at) — only a hash of the secret is stored.

evidence.title: The product goal
evidence.detail: For this demonstration we assume a business platform where integrations belong to an organization. This is not a verified strategy for any real product.

evidence.title: The change to identity and permissions
evidence.detail: The scenario assumes a new Org Key Registry and an extension of the existing Auth and Policy Engine. The diagram shows that model; it was not derived from code.

evidence.title: A new dependency from Auth to SQL
evidence.detail: To show the trade-off, we assume the domain reads SQL directly, and a ports-and-adapters rule. Both are inventions of this example, not findings from an audit.

evidence.title: More audit events
evidence.detail: The example adds key.created, key.rotated and key.revoked, reusing the existing Audit Log as the receiver. A real review would check who sends them, what the contract is, and who reads them.

evidence.title: Removing the compatibility path
evidence.detail: We assume the personal-token fallback is removed. The example deliberately leaves out a migration plan and customer data, so that the decision stays open for the product owner.

evidence.title: Error paths nobody has checked
evidence.detail: There are no results for tenant isolation, key revocation or a key-store outage. The list describes the checks that are needed; it does not mean those tests exist or passed.

evidence.title: Rotation schedule in the made-up PR
evidence.detail: Fictional example content. In a real review this record would quote the scheduled job, its interval, and what it writes, read from the diff at the exact head commit.

evidence.title: Hash-at-rest in the made-up PR
evidence.detail: Fictional example content. In a real review this record would name the column, the hashing routine and the migration that drops the plaintext token, all read in the source.
